headline: Ancient Mediterranean Trade Vessel Resurfaces After 4,500 Years
meta_description: Archaeologists discover the world's oldest shipwreck off Turkey's coast, dated to 4,400-4,700 years ago, with cargo jars still holding traces of ancient goods.
summary_short: A 10-meter trade ship resting 30 meters below the surface off Kekova Island has rewritten maritime history—and its ceramic pots still hold secrets.
body:
Archaeologists have uncovered the world's oldest shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, pushing back the boundaries of what we know about ancient maritime trade. Resting just 30 metres beneath the waves near Kekova Island in Antalya, the vessel dates to between 4,400 and 4,700 years ago—the Early Bronze Age, when the Great Pyramid itself was being constructed. Although the wooden hull has long since disintegrated, the ship's cargo tells an extraordinary story: more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae, still sit scattered across the underwater slope, and some remarkably still contain viscous residue from whatever goods they once held.

The 10-metre trading vessel was likely heading toward either the ancient city of Troy or the Minoan settlements in Crete when it met its fate in the notoriously treacherous waters around Kekova Island. Prof Hakan Öniz from Akdeniz University, who led the expedition, describes the wreck as "a time capsule at the bottom of the sea." By studying the distinctive shape of the amphorae—with their two handles, central ridge, and flat base—researchers matched the pottery to known artifacts from Egypt and the Middle East, definitively dating the find. Dr Karin Sowada, who examined the recovered pots, was astonished to discover substantial glossy residue still clinging inside; the cargo may have been olive oil, wine, or tree resins, though the jars may have been reused many times over their lives.

Beyond the technical achievement lies something more human: Öniz reflects that diving on the wreck brings to mind the sailors who crewed the vessel, the people who crafted and loaded the amphorae, and the families waiting ashore who never saw their loved ones return. The recovered artifacts will soon be displayed at the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya, offering visitors a tangible connection to lives lived millennia ago.
quick_facts: Shipwreck dated to 4,400–4,700 years ago, Early Bronze Age
Discovered 30 metres deep off Kekova Island, Antalya, Turkey
10-metre trade vessel carrying over 30 ceramic storage pots
Ceramic residue still visible inside some amphorae after thousands of years
Artifacts will display at new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum
